sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid page and JSON record for tani1255 (alt name Nyisunggu; subclassification comments cite Ross & Naess 2007, Naess & Boerger 2008, Francois 2009; refs: Tryon & Hackman 1983, UNESCO Atlas, Ethnologue 16, World Oral Literature Project; Glottolog lists no grammar, sketch or phonology).
sources.note: Bibliographic only: no grammar, sketch, phonology or dictionary of Tanimbili exists in Glottolog.

sources.citation: Lynch, John. 2000. Reconstructing Proto-Oceanic stress. Oceanic Linguistics 39(1):53-82. doi:10.2307/3623217
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: a digital copy exists, behind a library sign-in (also a publisher record (DOI), probably paywalled)
sources.note: l.99 lists '(b) Utupua-Vanikoro, located on the islands of Utupua and Vanikoro'; l.501-503: 'Buma (Tryon ToL) of the Utupua-Vanikoro family also has a system like this [penult stress, final if the final vowel is long], though it is rare in the Southern Oceanic linkage'. Nothing on Tanimbili or any Utupua-island language.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Tanimbili language' (wikitext via API, 2026-09-17); Wikidata Q3515188.
sources.note: Nothing on phonology; 15 speakers (1999); sole bibliography item is Tryon 1994 (Dutton & Tryon eds., Mouton de Gruyter, 611-648).

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell. 2009. Linguistic encounter and responses in the South Pacific. In Margaret Jolly, Serge Tcherkézoff & Darrell Tryon (eds), Oceanic Encounters: Exchange, Desire, Violence, 37-55. Canberra: ANU E Press. doi:10.22459/OE.07.2009.02
sources.note: No phonology content: language-contact essay; Tanimbili appears only in the census table 2.2 and in table 2.4 ('dog'.. Tanimbili.. kuli < Pileni kuli); refers readers to Tryon 1994:638-44 for irregular sound correspondences.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm & Åshild Næss. 2007. An Oceanic origin for Äiwoo, the language of the Reef Islands? Oceanic Linguistics 46(2):456-498.
sources.note: Comparative-historical paper establishing the Temotu subgroup with Utupua data; comparative tables may carry Tryon's Tanimbili forms; low chance of a stress statement but it is the work Glottolog cites for the subclassification.

sources.citation: Chan, Eugene S. L. (comp.). 2006 [data 1998]. Tanibili / Tanimbili. Numeral Systems of the World's Languages (MPI-EVA). Data: Brenda H. Boerger & Patterson Bagira, Solomon Islands Translation Advisory Group / SIL, 27 April 1998; IPA for 1-10, 100, 1000 from Darrell T. Tryon (ANU), 1988.
sources.note: Numerals 1-2000 (suo, buyu [mbuyu], bokwo [mbokwo], mafyo/mapio, kavili, kavilisuo.. vereŋalu '10', keilagu '100') with prenasalization shown in brackets; no stress or tone marks and no prosodic comment ('Tanibili has a decimal system'). Wordlist-only data, not a statement; shows SITAG/SIL and Tryon 1988 unpublished Tanibili data exist.

sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon. Sect. 5.2 'Utupua and Vanikoro'; family tree; Tryon's Buma (Vanikoro) sketch.
sources.note: Nothing on Tanimbili: the name occurs once, in the Utupua-Vanikoro family tree; Utupua is discussed only for subgrouping. The only Temotu sketch is Buma (Vanikoro), whose penultimate-stress statement is for a different island and subgroup, not applicable.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom & Darrell T. Tryon (eds). 1994. Language contact and change in the Austronesian world (Trends in Linguistics. Studies and Monographs 77). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter. ISBN 3-11-012786-5. [Held is the text of the whole 696-page volume although catalogued under Rivierre's chapter 'Contact-induced phonological complexification in New Caledonia', pp. 497-522, DOI 10.1515/9783110883091.497; chapters read for targets: Adelaar 'The classification of the Tamanic languages' 1-42; Bugenhagen 'Language change on Umboi Island' 43-108; Clark 'The Polynesian Outliers as a locus of language contact' 109-139; Dutton 'Motu-Koiarian contact in Papua New Guinea' 181-232; B. D. Grimes 'Cloves and nutmeg..' 251-274; Reid 'Unravelling the linguistic histories of Philippine Negritos' 443-475; Tryon 'Language contact and contact-induced language change in the Eastern Outer Islands, Solomon Islands' 611-648; Voorhoeve '..north Moluccas' 649-674.]
sources.note: No statement on stress or tone; morphosyntactic sketch, loans and segmental POC reflexes only.

sources.citation: Lynch, John & D. T. Tryon. 1985. Central-Eastern Oceanic: a subgrouping hypothesis. In Andrew Pawley & Lois Carrington (eds), Austronesian Linguistics at the 15th Pacific Science Congress, 31-52. Pacific Linguistics C-88. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C88.31
sources.note: Comparative morphosyntax (articles, possessives, verbal particles: 'UV: Asumboa, Tanimbili mbwa-ke if', 'Tanimbili has a personal article a') and consonant-correspondence tables (Tanimbili v,0 / t,s / j / 0,k..). No prosody; stress/accent/tone absent from the text.
sources.venue: Austronesian Linguistics at the 15th Pacific Science Congress

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands Languages: An Internal Classification (Pacific Linguistics C-72). Canberra: ANU. Tanimbili = wordlist no. 101 (Utupua), 50 speakers; name index (Tanabile, Tanambile, Tanebile, Gnisunggu); Utupua/Vanikoro reflex tables.
sources.note: Silent. Tanimbili appears in the census, name index, POC reflex tables (e.g. *niuR > Tanimbili nonio) and 300-item wordlist rows without stress marks; 'penultimate' does not occur; the only 'stress' tokens are 'It is stressed however' (rhetorical) and footnotes 'in unstressed position' on vowel reflexes of other languages.

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1982. Towards a classification of Solomon Islands languages. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 97-108. Pacific Linguistics C-74. Canberra: ANU. doi:10.15144/PL-C74.97
sources.note: Lexicostatistical classification plus 'broad lines of the phonological evidence' = POc consonant reflexes; for Utupua/Vanikoro only: 'Utupua appears to have lost reflexes of POC *R.. Nembao nie, Tanimbili nowio water.. Tanimbili nonio coconut' and POc *d > y in two of three Utupuan languages. No synchronic phonology; stress/accent/tone never mentioned.
sources.venue: Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages. Cambridge: CUP. 'Grammar of the Utupua Language', pp. 461-469 (= Asumboa [aua], from a MS by Rev. B. Teilo).
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 2234.7.25)
sources.note: Describes Asumboa, not Tanimbili; its 'Alphabet' and 'Sounds' sections carry no accent or stress statement.

sources.citation: Lackey, William James & Brenda H. Boerger. 2021. Reexamining the phonological history of Oceanic's Temotu subgroup. Oceanic Linguistics 60(2):367-411.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: digital copy at the publisher (paywalled); only the abstract or an excerpt is openly accessible
sources.note: Most recent phonological-historical treatment of the Temotu languages including Utupua; sibling checks report the abstract attributes syncope/truncation to prosodic effects, so it may state the stress pattern of the Utupua languages or cite a source for it.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. 1994. Language contact and contact-induced language change in the Eastern Outer Islands, Solomon Islands. In Tom Dutton & Darrell T. Tryon (eds), Language Contact and Change in the Austronesian World, 611-648. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only modern first-hand treatment of the three Utupua languages (Nembao, Asumboa, Tanimbili) by the only linguist who collected Tanimbili data; contains sound-correspondence tables (Google Books index) and may include phonological notes on stress. Google's index shows 'Tanimbili' and 'penultimate' both occur in the volume, unverified whether in the same passage.
sources.venue: Language Contact and Change in the Austronesian World
